schools across the country and how they result in -- how

loan debt as it regards to the COVID-19 pandemic, and the
current policy debate that is currently pending with

Higher Education Act and other
Consumer Financial Protection laws that are in place

practices in the market, as well as the laws, to look for
ways in which it can be improved to be more fair to
student loan borrowers; and then we write policy memos.

publicly and then to policymakers.

source_lines.text: Q    Ms. Yu, in -- in any of your work experience,
have you ever dealt with a situation where one loan
servicer takes over a student loan portfolio from another
loan servicer?
A    Yes, that -- that is a frequent occurrence.
Q    What has -- what has been your experience in
doing that?  What -- how many times has that come up?
A    So it does not -- I would say it's happened
about -- in the federal student loan context, it certainly
happens about a dozen times.  Most recently, we saw a
number of federal student loan servicers leave.  Navient
left and their loan portfolio transferred over to --
Q    Ms. Yu, you're starting to go fast again.
Apologies.
A    Sorry.
Most -- so most recently we saw, for example,
Navient left the Department of Education's loan portfolio,
and the loans were transferred to the company Maximus,
which runs a servicer called Aidvantage.  The -- PHEAA,
the loan servicer which operates under the name
FedLoan Servicing, also left the federal student loan
market.  Their loans were transferred to the servicer
Mohela.
There have been other smaller loan services which
have also left the market and which has resulted in
transfers of loan servicing to various different entities.
Also, loans are sometimes transferred from time to time.
This is also -- you know, occurs in the private student
loan market as well; however, the -- those occurrences
tend to be smaller and less spectacular with fewer
millions of borrowers transferred at any given moment.
Q    Thank you.
Do you have any experience with any of these
transfers in the private student loan market?
A    I do not recall -- I do -- I do not recall large
market transfers.  There may have been some when
Sallie Mae transitioned to Navient.  But like I said, they
happen typically on a much smaller scale than on the
Federal Student Loan scale.
Q    Thank you.
And whether they happen on a small scale or a
large scale, have you ever been involved in the nuts and
bolts of how they transfer the data from one servicer to
the other?  Or are you at a more 30,000-foot level?
MR. BLOOD:  Vague.
THE WITNESS:  Yes, I -- so what I understand --
I -- I have -- I have talked to servicers and the
Department of Education about what that process looks like
insofar as what the impact is to student loan borrowers.
For example, what has often happened is that
these loans as they are packaged to be transferred have to
be condensed into data files; right?  So many of these
servicers have multitudes of ways of -- of holding their
data.  Sometimes there are entire platforms that are
transferred.
For example, in the Navient to Maximus case,
the entire -- the -- Maximus took over the entire
servicing platform.  Whereas, in the case of
FedLoan Servicing to Mohela, loans had to be packaged.
And so I don't know that it's quite 30,000-square foot,
but I am not involved in the day-to-day operation of these
loans.  But I do a -- I -- I have an understanding of how
these transfers work insofar as what data is lost from --
from the student loan borrower's perspective and the risks
to student loan borrowers that can occur during a student
loan servicing transfer.
BY MR. PURCELL:
Q    Well, what are those risks?
A    The risks are that data loss.  There can be risks
of lost payments.  There can be risks -- risk of lost
communications between customer service representatives.
There can be the risk of lost files, that sort of thing.
I mean, basically, data is lost is -- is the main risk.
Also, there is often confusion amongst borrowers
about where to make payments, what they need to -- who
they need to interface with, as it is often quite opaque
to -- to the consumer who they should be discuss --
talking to about their loans at any given moment.
Q    And in your experience in dealing with the
student loans you've just described --
A    Yes.
Q    -- is it generally your experience that if one
student loan servicer stops servicing a portfolio, another
one will step in and take over?
A    That is -- that is generally how -- in my
experience, that is often what happens.
Q    Are you aware of any occasion when one student
loan servicer stepped away from servicing a portfolio and
nobody came in to take over the servicing?
Has that ever happened in your experience?
A    I am not aware of any instance where that has
occurred.
Q    Are you -- are you aware of any regulations that
apply to the manner in which student loan servicing data
is supposed to be transferred from the original servicer
to the follow-on servicer when there's a change in student
loan servicing?
A    There are a number of state laws that would
apply.  For example,
California State Student Loan Servicing Law I believe has
requirements about the data that must be transferred from
one servicer to another in -- in a -- when a transfer
occurs.  I believe that other states as well, but I don't
know them off the top of my head.
Q    Thank you.
In this case, of course, we're dealing with the
PEAKS loans that were in use at ITT; correct?
A    That's correct.
Q    Are you aware of any regulations that were
violated when the data was transferred by the original
servicer in this case, the Access Group, to my clients --
we'll refer to them as Vervent, but they were
First Associates at the time, in 2011?
A    Am I aware of any data that -- I'm sorry, can you
say that again?
Q    Sure.
Are you aware of any regulations that were
violated when the Access Group transferred the data for
the PEAKS loans to my client, Vervent, in 2011?
A    That's outside the scope of what I was asked to
look at in this case, and I don't have -- I don't have
access to the documents of what was transferred and
couldn't make an opinion about what rules were or were not
violated.
